final_answer:
No. The trial court most likely did not err (and a mandamus challenge would likely fail). LIMITATION: network egress blocked every full-text source (txcourts.gov, Justia, FindLaw, CourtListener, SCOTXblog), so I could not fetch or read any opinion. Under the citation firewall no authority is therefore cleared as verified final support; what follows rests on search-result descriptions of In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026) (Devine, J.), which appears to be this exact fact pattern (Prestige Consulting is a relator there), and should be confirmed against the opinion.

1. Governing rule (Texas). Texas applies a bright-line rule to side-switching nonlawyers (legal assistants/paralegals): the nonlawyer is conclusively presumed to have acquired the former client's confidences, and the new firm is disqualified unless it took minimal prophylactic measures, notably (a) instructing the nonlawyer at the inception of employment not to work on matters on which she worked in prior employment and not to disclose confidences, and (b) screening her from the matter. Per the search description of Zaidi, relators conceded there was no evidence of that admonishment here.

2. Application. Jones worked on the Apex side for about two years, in several hundred privileged communications and strategy meetings, and then worked on the same Apex-Prestige matter for the opposing firm on thirteen occasions and e-filed two documents. Smith Fullingham did not inquire about her prior work, gave no admonition, and screened her only after Apex complained in January 2023, long after she began working on the matter. Remedial measures taken after the conflict materialized do not satisfy the rule.

3. Arguments that the firm will raise. (a) She was not switching sides when hired and the conflict arose only in 2017 after the remand. Per the Zaidi description, the Court held that regardless of whether she was hired as a side-switcher, the firm must admonish the employee at or before she begins work on a later-arising conflicted matter, even years after hire. (b) Her claimed lack of recollection and the firm's assurance that she shared nothing do not rebut the conclusive presumption of acquired confidences, and the presumption of sharing is addressed by the required prophylactic measures, which were absent. (c) Waiver by delay from e-filing notifications naming her. Per the Zaidi description, notifications do not establish waiver as a matter of law; here Apex moved within about two months of learning in January 2023, which is prompt and unlikely to show waiver (waiver is a fact-dependent inquiry and the burden is on the party asserting it).

Bottom line: on these facts disqualification was likely proper; the firm's best (weak) arguments are fact-based waiver and unsupported assertions of non-disclosure. Confirm against the Zaidi opinion and the earlier Texas Supreme Court cases it builds on (e.g., Phoenix Founders v. Marshall, In re American Home Products, In re Columbia Valley Healthcare), none of which I was able to read.

claims.text: Texas applies a bright-line rule requiring disqualification of a firm that uses a side-switching nonlawyer on the same matter without minimal prophylactic measures (admonishment at inception and screening).
The admonishment duty applies even if the nonlawyer was not switching sides at hire and the conflict arose years later; post-complaint screening is insufficient.
E-filing notifications naming the nonlawyer do not establish waiver as a matter of law; a two-month delay is unlikely to show waiver.
